findings.breaking_input: A receipt with payload.lane = 'alice' and ts = '2026-10-14T00:00:00Z' plus a second receipt with deeper payload such as payload = { lane: 'bob', nested: { lane: 'alice' } } — the latter's top-level payload.lane is 'bob', so it names bob. More concretely: a receipt where payload.lane = 'alice' but ts is missing (undefined). Date.parse(undefined) = NaN, so it is skipped; but a receipt where payload.lane = 'alice' and ts = 'not-a-date' also skipped. Now consider a LIVE lane named only by a receipt whose ts = '2026-10-14T00:00:00Z' but whose id is missing (e.g. an old receipt with no id field). The lane is not stale, and last_id is null, so episodeOf = 'alice|never'. If an attacker appends a second receipt with payload.lane = 'alice' and ts = '2099-01-01' (far future), the lane still not stale, but episode key changes to future id. However the core flaw: deriveStale treats ANY object with payload.lane as a naming receipt, including receipts crafted by the owner-apply script or by a test that sets payload.lane on a rehearsal receipt. ADR-0079 says 'no receipt has named it', but there is no exclusion for rehearsal/test/fixture receipts; a rehearsal receipt with payload.lane marks a lane fresh and also resets the silence episode. Breaking input: a rehearsal receipt with kind='revenue.received', payload={lane:'growth', rehearsal:true}. The lane becomes non-stale, and the previous lane-stale incident episode is not lifted but the next run sees the lane fresh, so no alarm is raised despite real silence.
findings.why: deriveStale counts every receipt with a string payload.lane regardless of kind or marker fields. Rehearsal receipts, test harness events, and other non-real activity reset the 14-day clock and suppress the alarm entirely. This is defect-pattern (f) counts a rehearsal satisfies and (c) a gate reading its own output only partially fixed (own alarms excluded) — but any other receipt kind can carry a fake lane and revive a silent lane. The job's whole purpose is to notice silence; a forged or accidental 'lane' field on a rehearsal receipt defeats it silently.
findings.fix: In deriveStale, only count receipts whose kind is in a sanctioned activity set (e.g. phase.closed, kickoff.done, develop.started, slice.done, approval.requested) and reject any receipt that carries rehearsal/test/fixture markers — mirror the countsTowardLift logic. Also validate the receipt id is a string before using it in episodeOf; a missing id should make the receipt non-naming.

findings.breaking_input: A stale lane 'growth' with last_id null (never named). The job runs daily: first run computes episodeOf('growth', null) = 'growth|never' and raises one incident. Now an attacker writes a spine receipt (any kind, not lane-stale, maybe a note.logged) with payload.lane='growth' and ts = today, id = 'X'. Next run: the lane is fresh (last_id='X'), so no raise. Then the receipt is deleted from the spine (a transient or adversarial edit) — the lane falls silent again, last_id returns to null, and episodeOf = 'growth|never' again, which is in the raisedEpisodes set, so no duplicate raise is emitted. The lane is stale but never re-raised in its new silence episode because the episode key collides with the first ever episode.
findings.why: episodeOf uses 'never' as the key for any lane with no receipt. After one wake (even a deleted or temporary receipt) and re-silence, the episode is identical to the very first episode, so the dedup set suppresses the second raise forever. The job is meant to raise once per silence episode, but the 'never' key is not unique per episode — it collapses all never-named silences into one. This is defect-pattern (r) duplicate the emitter must quarantine, but the dedup is too aggressive and loses a needed alarm.
findings.fix: Make the episode key unique per silence run, e.g. include the run's derived_at timestamp or a monotonically increasing episode id derived from the spine's last receipt ts, not a bare 'never'. Store the last raised episode's derived_at in lane-stale.json and only dedup against that.
findings.twin_of: (r) a duplicate the emitter must quarantine

findings.breaking_input: An incident.raised with payload.class='lane-stale' and payload.silent_lane='growth' but payload.last_receipt_ts = 'garbage' (non-date string). The brief prints 'LIVE, no lane receipt since ever' even though last_receipt_ts is a string that is not a valid date — it slices to 'garbage'. More critically, an incident with silent_lane = '__proto__' or 'toString' is printed verbatim into the brief's markdown output; a lane name with markdown injection (e.g. '**bold**' or '[x](javascript:...)') is interpolated unescaped into the brief's text, so a crafted silent_lane can inject markdown or links into the needs-you section that a consumer (email, chat) renders.
findings.why: arc-brief takes payload.silent_lane and interpolates it directly into a template string with no escaping or length/character validation. The lane name comes from the spine, which any script can append. A malicious or accidental lane name with markdown metacharacters could alter the brief's rendering or exfiltrate content. The date slice is also not validated: a string without a date part is sliced arbitrarily, printing a garbage date instead of 'ever'.
findings.fix: Validate silent_lane against the LANE regex /^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$/; if it fails, print a generic 'unknown lane' placeholder. Validate last_receipt_ts by attempting Date.parse; fall back to 'ever' if not a valid date. Escape any markdown special characters in the emitted line.

findings.breaking_input: A lane-stale.json file where lanes['growth'] = { stale: true, last_ts: '2026-10-01', last_id: 'X' } but the JSON also has __proto__ pollution: JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}') returns an object with a polluted prototype. Then for every lane, d = derived.lanes[lane] looks up the normal prototype chain; if a lane name like 'constructor' or 'toString' is in the board, d may resolve to a function, and d && typeof d.stale === 'boolean' short-circuits, so stale stays null. More concretely, a lane named '__proto__' on the board (a valid lane name per the resolver? no, lane names are lowercase but '__proto__' is lowercase and matches the LANE regex) would get d = Object.prototype, and d && typeof d.stale === 'boolean' is false, returning null, but the real intent — an object with a literal __proto__ key — is lost because JSON.parse sets the prototype rather than an own property. A crafted state file can also have lanes = { 'some-lane': { stale: 'yes' } } — stale non-boolean is ignored, but stale_derived_at from derived_at is not validated against format.
findings.why: The state file is written by the job but is in a shared instance-state directory; any script can overwrite it. JSON.parse has the classic prototype-pollution hazard: keys like '__proto__', 'constructor', 'prototype' do not become own properties, so a malicious state file can alter the object's prototype, and later code that reads derived.lanes[lane] may resolve to Function.prototype or Object.prototype, returning truthy objects. The code checks Array.isArray(lanes) but not that lanes is a plain object without dangerous keys. This is the wrong-repo/spine class: the state file is attacker-influenceable instance state read without sanitisation.
findings.fix: After JSON.parse, walk the lanes object and reject or strip any key that is not a valid LANE name. Use Object.create(null) or copy to a fresh plain object, and validate each lane's stale is boolean, last_id/ts strings. Reject the whole file (return null) if it contains prototype keys.

findings.breaking_input: A board row where a data cell contains 'stale : true' (space before colon) or 'stale	: true' (tab before colon). The awk regex is /(^|[^a-z0-9-])stale[ \t]*[:=]/ — this matches 'stale :' because [ \t]* allows spaces between stale and the colon. But a cell value containing 'stale colons' such as 'x stale: y' is caught as a field, but the definition says only a hand-written field; a cell like 'the stale: value is 3' is flagged even though it is prose. More importantly, a cell value 'stale=yes' inside a code-fenced block is skipped correctly, but a cell value 'stale:' inside an HTML comment is skipped. However, a cell value 'stale:' on the separator row (row 2) is skipped because rows > 2 is required, and a table header cell equal to 'stale' with extra whitespace (e.g. '  stale  ' after clean()) is caught. The real hole: a table row where the first cell is 'stale:' but the row is actually a continuation of a code fence that was never closed — the fence toggles on ``` and off ```; a single unclosed ``` earlier makes all following lines treated as fenced and skipped, so a hand-written stale field after an unclosed fence is missed. Conversely a ``` inside a table cell (a literal pipe-line with ```) toggles the fence incorrectly, so a stale field after a legit ```-containing prose cell is flagged as the board.
findings.why: board-lint's fence handling is a single toggle on any line matching /^[ \t]*```/, with no rule that a fence must be at the start of a paragraph or that an odd number of fences is an error. A board with one stray triple-backtick in a cell (e.g. a code example in a next cell) flips the parser into fence mode and skips every subsequent table row, letting a hand-written stale: field pass. This is defect-pattern (a) markdown-contract parsing and (g) vacuous tests — the fence test only checks a cleanly paired fence.
findings.fix: Track fence state by counting backtick runs per line, and require an unclosed fence at EOF to be a FAIL (or at least a WARN plus treat the remaining lines as board). Also escape/parse inline code spanning cells.

findings.breaking_input: kickoff-lint --text 'some --base text' --lane memory --base base. The loop scans argv: it sees --text and skips its value ('some --base text' — one token if quoted, but if the shell splits it as three tokens 'some', '--base', 'text', the loop sees --text, skips i+1 which is 'some', then continues; at i=2 it sees '--base' and treats 'text' as its value, consuming it as baseRef and splices. Then the lane memory is preserved, but base becomes 'text', a non-existent ref, producing WARN [new-cycle-unknown] and skipping the gates. Worse, a free-text positional that equals '--base' (e.g. `kickoff-lint --lane memory original--base` where the value is a token '--base') is consumed as the flag, and its following token (possibly another flag) is eaten.
findings.why: The loop only skips the value of the known lane-parser flags (--lane, --root, --for, --print, --text) but it skips only ONE token as the value. --text can take a multi-word value that the shell has already split into several argv entries, and after that multi-word value, later tokens equal to '--base' are still treated as the flag. Also positionals that literally equal '--base' (free text the lane parser would otherwise ignore) are mis-consumed. This is defect-pattern (p) a flag value that looks like another flag, but incomplete: the skip of --text's value is one-token, not until the flag's value ends (which the lane parser defines as the rest of the sentence). The fix must treat --text's value as all remaining non-flag tokens, or parse strictly through parseLaneArgs.
findings.fix: Delegate all argument parsing to parseLaneArgs so it knows --text consumes the rest of the sentence (or a quoted value). Never scan argv independently; only extract --base before parseLaneArgs but stop at the first positional or a flag that starts with '-' that is not a lane-parser flag. Even better, push --base into parseLaneArgs as one of its own flags.
findings.twin_of: (p) a flag value that looks like another flag

findings.breaking_input: A debt-ledger.md whose first table has header '| # |' making hashIds=true, but then a later table (under later prose) has a different header without a '#' first column (e.g. '| what | where |'). The code never resets hashIds on a new header+separator: hashIds is set once when the first header+separator is seen and never updated. So the second table's rows are still read with hashIds=true, and its first cell (e.g. 'Fixed in PR 9') is treated as the row id, even though that table's rule should be the D-ordinal. Conversely, a file whose FIRST table has a non-# header but a later table has '#', misses the later table's ids. The splitRow and isSeparator logic only reads a header when a separator line follows immediately; a ledger that uses a separator row of '---' with varying lengths is fine, but a table whose header is followed by a blank line before the separator is skipped, and its data rows are read with the PREVIOUS table's hashIds.
findings.why: readDebtLedger sets hashIds once at the first header+separator and never revisits it. The ADR-0078 spec says ids come from the '#' cell only when the table's FIRST header is '#', else D-ordinal. For a file with multiple tables of different grammars (distribute appends rows under later prose with no repeated header, but a file could have two genuine tables), the second table's rows get mis-identified. This is defect-pattern (n) rows without a header, but the fix must reset state per table, not only handle the no-header-append case.
findings.fix: Track hashIds per table: when a header+separator is detected, recompute hashIds from that header. The append-without-header case (already handled) should reuse the last table's hashIds, not a stale value from a different earlier table.

findings.breaking_input: A ruling what: 'kernel freeze: no kickoff; launch, growth ARE exempt; but also memory is exempt'. parseRuling splits on ';' producing clauses: ['kernel freeze: no kickoff', 'launch, growth ARE exempt', ' but also memory is exempt']. The second clause matches /^(.+?) (?:is|are) exempt$/i and the third also matches, so both are processed and both add exemptions. But a clause like 'launch and growth are exempt' where 'launch and growth' contains ' and ' — the split on ',? and ' only handles the comma-and, not a plain ' and ' between two lanes. The items list after the replace becomes 'launch, growth' — okay. The hole: an exempt clause 'launch (note, with comma) are exempt' — the note contains a comma; the split on ',' inside the parens breaks it into 'launch (note' and ' with comma) are exempt', and the latter does not match any item shape, returning an error, failing closed. Even a legitimate note with a comma (e.g. 'engine (metered, authorized runs only)') refuses every lane. The grammar also fails on a lane name with uppercase (LANE_ITEM is [a-z]) even though the ruling may write 'Launch' — though the fixture uses lower-case, a real ruling could name a lane with a capital letter (e.g. 'Launch' as the board shows) — that fails closed.
findings.why: parseRuling splits the whole clause on ',' after replacing ', and ', but does not protect parenthesised notes from the comma split. A comma inside a note is a natural English construction. It also rejects uppercase lane names, though PROGRESS lane names are lowercase but the ruling prose might capitalise. This is defect-pattern (a) markdown-contract parsing: a strict grammar that fails on punctuation inside a quoted phrase. The fail-closed direction is safe but overly broad: it refuses ALL kickoffs, not just the exempt lane.
findings.fix: Split the exempt list only on commas that are OUTSIDE parentheses. For notes, extract the note up to the closing paren before splitting on commas. Normalise lane names to lowercase before matching.

findings.breaking_input: The base ref resolves and the lane's PROGRESS.md exists at the base, but git show returns a file with a CRLF line ending or a BOM. readHeader splits on /\r?\n/ and the cycle line becomes 'arc-x (Cycle 1)\r' — the \r is trimmed by the trailing [ \t]* in the regex, but if the file has a BOM at the start (UTF-8 BOM bytes), the first line's status/cycle regex does not match because of the BOM character. If the base file has a BOM, readHeader returns cycle null, baseIdentity is null, identity (working tree) is a non-null cycle, so state = 'new' — a mid-cycle lane with a BOM in the base is falsely refused. Conversely, if the working tree has a BOM, status regex fails, status null → not-live, and the gate skips, silently.
findings.why: readHeader does not strip a UTF-8 BOM, and git show may preserve CRLF/BOM exactly. A BOM on the base file makes the base look like it has no cycle header, triggering a false 'new' state; a BOM on the working tree makes status unreadable, which is treated as not-live (silent skip). This is the markdown-contract parsing class — a leading invisible character defeats an exact-match regex.
findings.fix: Strip a leading BOM (and CR before \n) from the text before splitting, or use readHeader on both sides after normalising line endings and removing a BOM.

findings.breaking_input: A directory initiatives/ has a subdirectory 'foo' with a PROGRESS.md that is a symlink to a directory or a special file (e.g. /dev/null). existsSync(join(dir, lane, 'PROGRESS.md')) returns true for a symlink to a regular file, but if it is a symlink loop or points to a device, readFileSync throws EISDIR or ELOOP, which is not caught in readLanes — it propagates and crashes the whole job, so a single broken lane directory prevents the stale derivation for ALL lanes, and the job exits non-zero (not 2 or 0), so no state file is written and no alarms are raised. The daily job is supposed to be resilient; a stray symlink or permissions issue in one lane halts the entire board's noticing.
findings.why: readLanes reads every PROGRESS.md with readFileSync inside a .map with no try/catch. A lane directory that exists but whose PROGRESS.md is unreadable (permission, symlink loop, special file) throws and aborts main() before the state write. This is defect-pattern (i) one null for two failures — unreadable vs absent both need distinct handling, but here unreadable is a crash, and the net effect is the same as the freeze gate skipping: no alarm.
findings.fix: Wrap the readFileSync/readHeader in try/catch per lane; skip lanes where the header is unreadable, or treat them as 'unknown-live' and still derive stale (since the job cannot confirm it is not LIVE, fail closed to stale would be safer). At minimum, do not crash on one bad lane.
